title: A unified symmetry framework for spin–ferroelectric coupling in altermagnetic multiferroics

paper_content.abstract: Altermagnetic multiferroics, hosting coexisting spin-splitting bands and ferroelectric polarization, offer a promising route to magnetoelectric coupling beyond conventional relativistic spin–orbit mechanism. However, the lack of a unified principle connecting ferroelectric switching symmetry to spin-band topology has impeded rational material design. Here, we establish a universal symmetry-based framework that classifies all possible spin–ferroelectric couplings in altermagnets into three fundamental types: decoupling, pseudo-time-reversal coupling, and asymmetric momentum mapping. This classification stems directly from the relation between ferroelectric switching operators and the spin Laue group, creating a decisive symmetry-to-function paradigm. First-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 confirm the framework, showing that 3 distinct ferroelectric switching paths produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions and discriminable electrical transport signatures. The universality of the framework is further validated in BiFeO3. Our work provides a predictive design principle for voltage-programmable spintronics, effectively transforming ferroelectric symmetry from a structural descriptor into a dynamic functional control knob for altermagnetic spin states.
paper_content.introduction:
Altermagnetic multiferroics—materials that simultaneously host altermagnetic and ferroelectric orders—represent a new frontier in the design of strongly coupled magnetoelectric systems1–4. Conventional multiferroics are often limited by the inherent separation between the coexisting ferroelectric and magnetic orders, resulting in weak magnetoelectric coupling that typically depends on spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as an indirect mediator5,6. In contrast, altermagnetic multiferroics feature opposite spin sublattices within the crystal lattice, which are connected by rotation or mirror symmetries, while prohibiting connection through translational or inversion symmetries7–15. This gives rise to momentum-space spin splitting in the compensated magnetic ordering, which is naturally compatible with the inversion symmetry breaking induced by the ferroelectric. Central to this is the spatial symmetry, which serves as a key parameter for geometrically coupling the spin-split electronic bands of altermagnets with the switchable ferroelectric polarization, bypassing the reliance on SOC. This intrinsic symmetry coupling offers a direct route to achieving robust magnetoelectric responses, fulfilling the critical requirements for next-generation spintronic memory and logic devices16–27.

Recent theoretical studies have shown that in various low-dimensional and three-dimensional altermagnetic multiferroic materials, ferroelectric switching can reversibly modulate the spin texture without altering the global magnetic ordering28–32. This offers an ideal platform for electric-field control of spin states and highlight promising prospects for low-power, nonvolatile spintronic applications. However, it is important to note that this coupling is subject to strict symmetry constraints. For example, in some altermagnetic multiferroics, it has been found that the switching of ferroelectric polarization does not affect the spin electronic bands of the altermagnetic29,31. This suggests that the coexistence of ferroelectric and altermagnetic does not necessarily lead to their coupling, and the symmetry conditions that govern whether such coupling occurs remain unclear. More fundamentally, a unified theoretical framework is still lacking to systematically describe how ferroelectric switching modulates altermagnetic spin splitting. In particular, symmetry-based classification criteria that can predict spin responses under different switching operations remain underdeveloped, hindering rational material design and functional optimization.

To address this gap, we develop a group-theoretic classification of spin–ferroelectric coupling in altermagnets. Our analysis identifies three fundamental response types—Type I: spin–ferroelectric decoupling, and Type II: pseudo-time-reversal (pseudo-spin-flip) coupling, and Type III: non-symmetric momentum mapping—each determined by the relationship between the ferroelectric switching operator and the crystal’s spin Laue group. These theoretical predictions are first confirmed through first-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 and subsequently validated in BiFeO3 as a prototypical 3D system, in which distinct ferroelectric switching paths are shown to produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions.

This work establishes a unified symmetry-guided framework for understanding and designing altermagnetic multiferroics with tailored magnetoelectric functionality. The distinct spin-band reconstructions further give rise to discriminable electrical transport signatures, enabling simple electrical measurements to serve as direct experimental fingerprints of the three symmetry-determined coupling types. Thus, the framework not only offers fundamental theoretical insight but also provides a practical material platform for the development of voltage-programmable, low-power spintronic devices.

During this process, the spins remain unchanged in real space, but exhibit distinct responses in momentum space. By matching the real-space ferroelectric switching operation with the Laue group in momentum space, three distinct types of effects on the spin-resolved band structure E(s,k) of an altermagnet are observed, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

We further obtained numerical results from the tight-binding model constructed under the 2/m Laue group (Supplementary Fig. S1), which are in perfect agreement with the aforementioned group-theoretical classification. This further validates the impact of different ferroelectric switching symmetries on the three characteristic types of spin bands in altermagnetism.

Notably, in altermagnets, the set {E, I} always belong to H. Thus, any ferroelectric switching operation involving only inversion leaves the spin spectrum unaffected and is inherently of Type I. This is particularly relevant in 2D systems, where the z-component is a pseudoscalar, rendering the set {C , M} effectively equivalent to {E, I}. Therefore, operations O {I, C , M } in 2D systems are invariably classified as Type I, remaining decoupled from spin in any Laue group.

First-principles validation in 2D bilayer MnPS3
First-principles calculations offer a realistic platform for validating the theoretical classification of spin–ferroelectric locking. We selected bilayer MnPS3 as a candidate system, where sliding ferroelectricity in van der Waals bilayers exhibits exceptional tunability. Unlike conventional ferroelectrics with a single, fixed switching path, polarization reversal in this system can be realized through multiple layer-sliding trajectories defined by distinct symmetry operations. This intrinsic flexibility makes sliding ferroelectrics an ideal platform for systematically exploring different ferroelectric switching symmetries within a single material family.

Starting from a monolayer of MnPS3 with Néel-type antiferromagnetic ordering (its relevant structural and magnetic properties are presented in Supplementary Fig. S2), we construct the bilayer by applying the mapping {M z |τ o } together with an out-of-plane translation τ, resulting in a crystallographic point group of m and a crystallographic Laue group of 2/m, with the full set of symmetry operations G={E, C , I, M}. The halving subgroup H={E, I} preserves each spin sublattice. Consequently, the system is governed by the altermagnetic group R AM =[E||{E, I}]+[C ||{C , M }], which generates the characteristic alternating sign pattern of spin splitting in the Brillouin zone. In this construction, the sliding ferroelectric polarization P is controlled by the in-plane translation vector τ o of the top layer relative to the bottom layer. DFT total-energy scans identify a global maximum for the paraelectric phase at τ =(0,0), along with six degenerate global minima for the ferroelectric phase at τ {(va,0), (0,vb), (va,vb) | v=±1/3}, as shown in Fig. 2b, leading to uncompensated interfacial charge transfer and a combined polarization of 0.92 μC/m (in-plane) and 0.26 μC/m (out-of-plane), as demonstrated by the charge difference between the paraelectric and ferroelectric phases in Supplementary Fig. S3. We identify three transition paths: path 1 maintains the crystal’s mirror symmetry orientation and reverses only the out-of-plane component with an energy barrier of 11.8 meV/f.u., while paths 2 and 3 rotate the crystal’s mirror symmetry orientation by π/3, switch both in-plane and out-of-plane components. The energy barriers for paths 2 and 3 are degenerate, both at 9.2 meV/f.u. (Fig. 2c). The theory of bilayer stacking ferroelectricity (BSF) provides a method for selectively choosing sliding paths using an external electric field33, allowing for controllable polarization switching, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S4.

To comprehensively investigate possible ferroelectric switching symmetries in the system, we employ two distinct interlayer antiferromagnetic configurations as analysis platforms. The two configurations are nearly degenerate in energy (difference ∼0.22 meV), indicating weak interlayer exchange coupling. Under these conventions, we obtain four representative ferroelectric switching operations, as summarized in Fig. 2d. Equations (11, 13) correspond to ferroelectric transition path 1, while (12) and (14) correspond to path 2. Their effects on the altermagnetic spin spectrum are as follows. In Equation (11), M acts in the 2D Brillouin zone as equivalent to the identity element E H, realizing Type I—spin–ferroelectric decoupling. Since the M operation reduces to the identity in the 2D momentum space, it imposes no additional constraints and is therefore not considered further in Equations (12)–(14). Equation (12) involves the C operation. Since C =G, it induces a Type III — non-symmetric mapping, geometrically rotating the momentum-space spin texture by π/3. In Equation (13), M y AH enacts Type II—pseudo-time-reversal coupling, producing a global reversal of spin labels. Finally, Equation (14), the composite M C , combines Type II and Type III: it applies a pseudo-time-reversal–like inversion of the spin spectrum, followed by a π/3 rotation in k-space. The resulting geometric and spectral reconstructions are illustrated in Fig. 3. The complete electronic structures, including the conduction bands for the L and L magnetic configurations, are presented in Supplementary Fig. S6. In addition, the ferroelectric switching along path 3 exhibits a similar effect to that of path 2, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S7. This result further confirms the three characteristic effects of ferroelectric switching on the spin-resolved band structure, providing a concrete material realization and a physical basis for the theoretical classification of spin-ferroelectric coupling.

Within the Boltzmann transport framework, the band structure—by governing the nonequilibrium distribution function—directly translates into electrical signals, providing a direct electrical response measurement to probe the aforementioned band mapping relationship. We accordingly calculated the spin-resolved charge conductivity σ , as shown in Fig. 4. When a current-driving electric field is applied along the mirror-symmetric x direction, spin-up and spin-down channels generate transverse Hall currents of opposite signs along the y direction. During ferroelectric switching along path 1, the spin Hall current follows the symmetry-locked characteristics of Type I or Type II coupling, either remaining unchanged in the L magnetic ordering according to Equation (11), or reversing its overall sign in the L magnetic ordering according to Equation (13). In contrast, along path 2, the involvement of an additional C =G symmetry modifies the anisotropic characteristics of the spin-band, thereby giving rise to a Type III strongly direction-asymmetric transverse current response in the L and L magnetic orderings, as described by Equations (12) and (14). This behavior is likewise manifested during the ferroelectric transition along path 3, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S8. Such distinct transport behavior provides a functional verification of the theoretical classification, clearly distinguishing the three representative coupling types identified in the symmetric analysis, and establishes an experimentally accessible electrical criterion for identifying different ferroelectric switching pathways.

Proof of universality using BiFeO3 as a 3D exemplar
To further demonstrate the generality of our symmetry-based framework beyond 2D systems, we extend our analysis to a classic 3D multiferroic material, G-type antiferromagnetic BiFeO3 multiferroics with R3c space group, the altermagnetism was confirmed recently32. From a symmetry perspective, the corresponding crystallographic Laue group of this system is 3m, and its complete set of symmetry operations is G={E, I, C 3[111] , C2 3[111] , S 3[111] , S2 3[111] , C 2[-110] , C 2[01-1] , C 2[10-1] , M[-110] , M[01-1] , M[10-1] }. The halving subgroup H={E, I, C 3[111] , C2 3[111] , S 3[111] , S2 3[111] } preserves each spin sublattice. Therefore, the system is described by the altermagnetic group R AM =[E||{E, I, C 3[111] , C2 3[111] , S 3[111] , S2 3[111] }]+[C 2 ||{C 2[-110] , C 2[01-1] , C 2[10-1] , M[-110] , M[01-1] , M[10-1] }], representing a g-wave altermagnetic system, as shown in Fig. 5a, b.

In bulk BiFeO3, the R3c crystal structure arises from Pm3 m by the condensation of two primary order parameters: a polar distortion along the [111] direction and a rotation of the oxygen octahedra along the [111] direction, described by the R+ 4 irreducible representation. For polarization switching achieved by independent displacement of Bi3+ ions (referred to as path 1), the overall effect is equivalent to an inversion operation O =I, i.e., [E||I]P=P’ (Fig. 5b). However, in certain conditions, polarization switching maybe accompanied by the rotation of the oxygen octahedra (referred to as path 2)34. In this case, inversion symmetry cannot map the lattice structure while preserving the system’s magnetic ordering; instead, path 2 affects the system in an O =C 2[-110] manner, i.e., [E||C 2[-110]]P=P’ (Fig. 5b). According to Equation 9, the path 1, where O H, does not alter the spin splitting during polarization reversal, and is classified as Type I (decoupled). Path 2, where O AH, maps the opposite spin channels and is classified as Type II (pseudo-time-reversal coupling). The band structure calculations shown in Fig. 5 clearly confirm these two distinct responses.

This analysis not only emphasizes that the spin splitting control in BiFeO3 is directly related to octahedral rotation rather than polarization switching, providing an intuitive symmetry perspective for electric control of spin splitting in BiFeO3, but also clarifies the universal applicability of this symmetry mechanism in various multiferroic materials. By identifying the symmetry of the ferroelectric switching operation, one can predict and classify its magnetoelectric coupling functionality, independent of the specific system under study.
paper_content.methods: The atomic properties and electronic structure of the materials were calculated using first-principles simulations within density functional theory (DFT)35,36. The projected augmented wave pseudopotentials method, as implemented in the Vienna Abinitio Simulation Package (VASP)37,38 was employed. The exchange-correlation energy was calculated using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form39, and the plane wave cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. A Hubbard U =4 eV with the Dudarev parametrization was applied to properly describe the localization of Mn 3d orbitals40. The semiempirical DFT-D3 method was used to include the van der Waals interaction41. For MnPS3 calculations, a centered 9×9×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was used42. To eliminate periodic boundary effects, the vacuum space between adjacent slabs was set to exceed 15 Å along the z direction. Using the conjugate gradient method, the plane lattice constant and atomic coordinates were fully relaxed until the energy and force converged to 10−6 and 10−2 eV/Å, respectively. The Berry-phase method was employed to evaluate polarization magnitude43, and the ferroelectric transition switching pathway was obtained using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method44. The spin-resolved charge conductivity was calculated using Boltzmann transport theory within the constant-relaxation-time approximation as implemented in the Wannier90 package45, with the electronic temperature and relaxation time set to 300 K and 1 ps, respectively. The lattice structure was visualized using VESTA46.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I have carefully read manuscript titled “A unified Symmetry Framework for Spin Ferroelectric Coupling in Altermagnetic Multiferroics”. Authors have described concept of altermagnetic multiferroelectric which would represent both altermagnetism and ferroelectricity, both individually holding interesting and useful properties by its own. Coexistence is often debated, while coupling, especially concepts like the coupling factor is even more controversial within the community. Authors have tried to come up with theory to explain all possible spin–ferroelectric couplings in altermagnets, again a topic of discussion and interest. Authors have taken into consideration the example of MnPS3 as example system showing sliding ferroelectricity and tried explaining possible ferroelectric switching states, possible pathways and resultant spin-band splitting and possible electric signature. Hypothesis of the manuscript and structure is sound, even though not groundbreaking, but useful for the community considering its systematic representation of possible mechanisms. Ferroelectric materials are getting lot of attention in recent months for transistors and MRAMs and coupled properties with altermagnetism would be an interesting avenue for research community. The referee provides an overall positive evaluation of this work, while also highlighting notable concerns regarding its possible similarity to recent comparable publications. The following comments are provided to help enhance its quality, depth, and accessibility for members of the ferroic research community, with particular attention to those working in ferroelectricity.
1) Can authors explain clear distinctions between recently published PRB: (cid:1)-type antiferromagnetic BiFeO3 is a multiferroic (cid:2)-wave altermagnet (https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/v3fg-6smc) with this manuscript. Is this manuscript a subset of the previously mentioned publication? The publication of this work in a renowned journal such as Nature Communications is highly questionable without adequate justification.

4) In Group-Theoretical Analysis of Spin–Ferroelectric Locking section, can authors comments on general observations for standard ferroelectric systems (so called 3D, other than 2D) which may have similar altermagnetic coupled ferroelectric properties (if any) and if not why not?

Good Potential reference, Figure 1 of Ultrafast high-endurance memory based on sliding ferroelectrics (DOI: 10.1126/science.adp3575).
7) What kind of energy distribution is mentioned in figure 3B? Can authors explain why Path1 has higher barrier energy for switching compared to path2 or 3? Authors should add clear schematics to show L1 and L2 magnetic order atleast in SI for clear representation.
8) What stimulus is applied to achieve this sliding ferroelectric switching? Is it mechanical or electrical? Is it out of plane or in-plane application of stimulus?
9) Can authors careful map each of equation 11,12,13 and 14 to show its corresponding structure in figure 4?
10) Authors should add xyz coordinates in figure 5 to indicate coordinates system.
11) Similar comments for Figure 5. Authors should try to correlate equations and corresponding figure 4 and figure 5 to clearly show connections between different sections of the manuscript.
12) Can authors add comments about all the presented theory for its applicability or limitations for prototypical multiferroic (possible altermagnetic) 3D ferroelectric such as BiFeO3 or any other relevant standard system in ferroelectric world in last portion of the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Sun and co-workers present a symmetry analysis enabling the prediction of couplings between spins and ferroelectric displacements in altermagnets. They identify three different types of coupling: a first mechanism in which spins and ferroelectric displacements are decoupled, and two additional paths in which polarization reversal can reverse the spin texture. Using these couplings, they further demonstrate that, in one of these mechanisms, the spin texture can generate a finite charge current. This could be highly desirable for spintronic applications.
Overall, I find the paper interesting and relevant for the spintronics community. Nevertheless, I also find it rather technical in places and perhaps too specialized for a broad audience. In addition, I miss a clear recipe for identifying compounds that satisfy the optimal criteria — the reader is left somewhat “starved” at the end. Therefore, I feel the manuscript falls a bit short for publication in Nature Communications. I would instead recommend submission to a more specialized journal such as Physical Review Letters or a similar outlet. The paper also appears to be a modified manuscript transferred from another journal, with “Section IV (Methods)” unexpectedly placed in the middle of the text.
Beyond these comments, I also find the duplication between the tight-binding and density-functional-theory approaches somewhat puzzling. Wouldn’t it be simpler to present a single test case based solely on DFT? I list below a few additional remarks that the authors may find relevant:
(I) Please clarify the antiferromagnetic orders used in the calculations.
(II) The units used for the spontaneous polarization are unusual and likely incorrect (µC·cm-2 are standard).
(III) Energy barriers are discussed in meV per formula unit, whereas Fig. 3(c) uses a different normalization.
(IV) Sketches for the different pathways are highly recommended, as these are not easy to infer from Fig. 3(b) alone.

Sun and co-workers present a symmetry analysis enabling the prediction of couplings between
spins and ferroelectric displacements in altermagnets. They identify three different types of
coupling: a first mechanism in which spins and ferroelectric displacements are decoupled, and two
additional paths in which polarization reversal can reverse the spin texture. Using these couplings,
they further demonstrate that, in one of these mechanisms, the spin texture can generate a finite
charge current. This could be highly desirable for spintronic applications.
Overall, I find the paper interesting and relevant for the spintronics community. Nevertheless, I
also find it rather technical in places and perhaps too specialized for a broad audience. In addition,
I miss a clear recipe for identifying compounds that satisfy the optimal criteria — the reader is left
somewhat “starved” at the end. Therefore, I feel the manuscript falls a bit short for publication in
Nature Communications. I would instead recommend submission to a more specialized journal
such as Physical Review Letters or a similar outlet. The paper also appears to be a modified
manuscript transferred from another journal, with “Section IV (Methods)” unexpectedly placed in
the middle of the text.

appreciate the positive assessment of our work's relevance to the spintronics community.
We fully acknowledge the concern regarding the technical nature of the original manuscript. In
response, we have undertaken a comprehensive revision aimed at making the content more
accessible to a broad readership while strengthening its practical utility. Importantly, our symmetry
framework does provide a clear, experimentally actionable “recipe”: based on different spin-
ferroelectric coupling types, it directly predicts distinct electrical transport signatures, such as the
spin Hall response. This bridges theoretical symmetry analysis with tangible experimental
validation.
To address the reviewer’s suggestions, we have implemented the following key improvements in
the revised manuscript:
1. Enhanced clarity and accessibility:
(1) The Introduction has been rewritten to provide a more intuitive physical overview,
(2) Technical derivations and the detailed tight-binding model have been moved to
Supplementary Information, allowing the main text to focus on conceptual understanding
and physical implications.
(3) Figures have been enriched with clearer labels, schematics, and coordinate annotations to
guide readers through the symmetry mappings and switching pathways.
2. Expanded discussion on material applicability:
(1) We have added a dedicated section on BiFeO as a 3D exemplar, demonstrating how our
3
symmetry classification applies directly to a well-known multiferroic system. This
illustrates the framework's generality beyond 2D materials and provides a concrete
example of how to identify coupling types in real compounds.
(2) The discussion of sliding ferroelectric mechanisms, symmetry mapping, and switching
pathways has been strengthened to offer clearer guidance on how different switching
operations relate to observable spin–texture reconstructions.
3. Structural improvements:
(1) The “Methods” section has been relocated to its proper position after the Conclusion.
(2) The flow of the manuscript has been reorganized to better connect symmetry analysis,
computational validation, and transport predictions.
We believe these revisions have significantly increased the manuscript’s appeal and readability for
a wide scientific audience, while preserving the rigorous theoretical foundation that specialists will

## Abstract

Altermagnetic multiferroics, hosting coexisting spin-splitting bands and ferroelectric polarization, offer a promising route to magnetoelectric coupling beyond conventional relativistic spin–orbit mechanism. However, the lack of a unified principle connecting ferroelectric switching symmetry to spin-band topology has impeded rational material design. Here, we establish a universal symmetry-based framework that classifies all possible spin–ferroelectric couplings in altermagnets into three fundamental types: decoupling, pseudo-time-reversal coupling, and asymmetric momentum mapping. This classification stems directly from the relation between ferroelectric switching operators and the spin Laue group, creating a decisive symmetry-to-function paradigm. First-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 confirm the framework, showing that 3 distinct ferroelectric switching paths produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions and discriminable electrical transport signatures. The universality of the framework is further validated in BiFeO3. Our work provides a predictive design principle for voltage-programmable spintronics, effectively transforming ferroelectric symmetry from a structural descriptor into a dynamic functional control knob for altermagnetic spin states.

---

## Introduction

Altermagnetic multiferroics—materials that simultaneously host altermagnetic and ferroelectric orders—represent a new frontier in the design of strongly coupled magnetoelectric systems1–4. Conventional multiferroics are often limited by the inherent separation between the coexisting ferroelectric and magnetic orders, resulting in weak magnetoelectric coupling that typically depends on spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as an indirect mediator5,6. In contrast, altermagnetic multiferroics feature opposite spin sublattices within the crystal lattice, which are connected by rotation or mirror symmetries, while prohibiting connection through translational or inversion symmetries7–15. This gives rise to momentum-space spin splitting in the compensated magnetic ordering, which is naturally compatible with the inversion symmetry breaking induced by the ferroelectric. Central to this is the spatial symmetry, which serves as a key parameter for geometrically coupling the spin-split electronic bands of altermagnets with the switchable ferroelectric polarization, bypassing the reliance on SOC. This intrinsic symmetry coupling offers a direct route to achieving robust magnetoelectric responses, fulfilling the critical requirements for next-generation spintronic memory and logic devices16–27.

Recent theoretical studies have shown that in various low-dimensional and three-dimensional altermagnetic multiferroic materials, ferroelectric switching can reversibly modulate the spin texture without altering the global magnetic ordering28–32. This offers an ideal platform for electric-field control of spin states and highlight promising prospects for low-power, nonvolatile spintronic applications. However, it is important to note that this coupling is subject to strict symmetry constraints. For example, in some altermagnetic multiferroics, it has been found that the switching of ferroelectric polarization does not affect the spin electronic bands of the altermagnetic29,31. This suggests that the coexistence of ferroelectric and altermagnetic does not necessarily lead to their coupling, and the symmetry conditions that govern whether such coupling occurs remain unclear. More fundamentally, a unified theoretical framework is still lacking to systematically describe how ferroelectric switching modulates altermagnetic spin splitting. In particular, symmetry-based classification criteria that can predict spin responses under different switching operations remain underdeveloped, hindering rational material design and functional optimization.

To address this gap, we develop a group-theoretic classification of spin–ferroelectric coupling in altermagnets. Our analysis identifies three fundamental response types—Type I: spin–ferroelectric decoupling, and Type II: pseudo-time-reversal (pseudo-spin-flip) coupling, and Type III: non-symmetric momentum mapping—each determined by the relationship between the ferroelectric switching operator and the crystal’s spin Laue group. These theoretical predictions are first confirmed through first-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 and subsequently validated in BiFeO3 as a prototypical 3D system, in which distinct ferroelectric switching paths are shown to produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions.

This work establishes a unified symmetry-guided framework for understanding and designing altermagnetic multiferroics with tailored magnetoelectric functionality. The distinct spin-band reconstructions further give rise to discriminable electrical transport signatures, enabling simple electrical measurements to serve as direct experimental fingerprints of the three symmetry-determined coupling types. Thus, the framework not only offers fundamental theoretical insight but also provides a practical material platform for the development of voltage-programmable, low-power spintronic devices.

Unlike conventional ferroelectrics with a single, fixed switching path, polarization reversal in this system can be realized through multiple layer-sliding trajectories defined by distinct symmetry operations. This intrinsic flexibility makes sliding ferroelectrics an ideal platform for systematically exploring different ferroelectric switching symmetries within a single material family.

## Methods

The atomic properties and electronic structure of the materials were calculated using first-principles simulations within density functional theory (DFT)35,36. The projected augmented wave pseudopotentials method, as implemented in the Vienna Abinitio Simulation Package (VASP)37,38 was employed. The exchange-correlation energy was calculated using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form39, and the plane wave cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. A Hubbard U =4 eV with the Dudarev parametrization was applied to properly describe the localization of Mn 3d orbitals40. The semiempirical DFT-D3 method was used to include the van der Waals interaction41. For MnPS3 calculations, a centered 9×9×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was used42. To eliminate periodic boundary effects, the vacuum space between adjacent slabs was set to exceed 15 Å along the z direction. Using the conjugate gradient method, the plane lattice constant and atomic coordinates were fully relaxed until the energy and force converged to 10−6 and 10−2 eV/Å, respectively. The Berry-phase method was employed to evaluate polarization magnitude43, and the ferroelectric transition switching pathway was obtained using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method44. The spin-resolved charge conductivity was calculated using Boltzmann transport theory within the constant-relaxation-time approximation as implemented in the Wannier90 package45, with the electronic temperature and relaxation time set to 300 K and 1 ps, respectively. The lattice structure was visualized using VESTA46.

## Abstract

Altermagnetic multiferroics, hosting coexisting spin-splitting bands and ferroelectric polarization, offer a promising route to magnetoelectric coupling beyond conventional relativistic spin–orbit mechanism. However, the lack of a unified principle connecting ferroelectric switching symmetry to spin-band topology has impeded rational material design. ## Introduction

Altermagnetic multiferroics—materials that simultaneously host altermagnetic and ferroelectric orders—represent a new frontier in the design of strongly coupled magnetoelectric systems1–4. Conventional multiferroics are often limited by the inherent separation between the coexisting ferroelectric and magnetic orders, resulting in weak magnetoelectric coupling that typically depends on spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as an indirect mediator5,6. In contrast, altermagnetic multiferroics feature opposite spin sublattices within the crystal lattice, which are connected by rotation or mirror symmetries, while prohibiting connection through translational or inversion symmetries7–15. This gives rise to momentum-space spin splitting in the compensated magnetic ordering, which is naturally compatible with the inversion symmetry breaking induced by the ferroelectric. Central to this is the spatial symmetry, which serves as a key parameter for geometrically coupling the spin-split electronic bands of altermagnets with the switchable ferroelectric polarization, bypassing the reliance on SOC. This intrinsic symmetry coupling offers a direct route to achieving robust magnetoelectric responses, fulfilling the critical requirements for next-generation spintronic memory and logic devices16–27.

Recent theoretical studies have shown that in various low-dimensional and three-dimensional altermagnetic multiferroic materials, ferroelectric switching can reversibly modulate the spin texture without altering the global magnetic ordering28–32. This offers an ideal platform for electric-field control of spin states and highlight promising prospects for low-power, nonvolatile spintronic applications. However, it is important to note that this coupling is subject to strict symmetry constraints. For example, in some altermagnetic multiferroics, it has been found that the switching of ferroelectric polarization does not affect the spin electronic bands of the altermagnetic29,31. This suggests that the coexistence of ferroelectric and altermagnetic does not necessarily lead to their coupling, and the symmetry conditions that govern whether such coupling occurs remain unclear. More fundamentally, a unified theoretical framework is still lacking to systematically describe how ferroelectric switching modulates altermagnetic spin splitting. In particular, symmetry-based classification criteria that can predict spin responses under different switching operations remain underdeveloped, hindering rational material design and functional optimization.

To address this gap, we develop a group-theoretic classification of spin–ferroelectric coupling in altermagnets. Our analysis identifies three fundamental response types—Type I: spin–ferroelectric decoupling, and Type II: pseudo-time-reversal (pseudo-spin-flip) coupling, and Type III: non-symmetric momentum mapping—each determined by the relationship between the ferroelectric switching operator and the crystal’s spin Laue group. These theoretical predictions are first confirmed through first-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 and subsequently validated in BiFeO3 as a prototypical 3D system, in which distinct ferroelectric switching paths are shown to produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions.

This work establishes a unified symmetry-guided framework for understanding and designing altermagnetic multiferroics with tailored magnetoelectric functionality. The distinct spin-band reconstructions further give rise to discriminable electrical transport signatures, enabling simple electrical measurements to serve as direct experimental fingerprints of the three symmetry-determined coupling types. Thus, the framework not only offers fundamental theoretical insight but also provides a practical material platform for the development of voltage-programmable, low-power spintronic devices.

## Methods

The atomic properties and electronic structure of the materials were calculated using first-principles simulations within density functional theory (DFT)35,36. The projected augmented wave pseudopotentials method, as implemented in the Vienna Abinitio Simulation Package (VASP)37,38 was employed. The exchange-correlation energy was calculated using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form39, and the plane wave cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. A Hubbard U =4 eV with the Dudarev parametrization was applied to properly describe the localization of Mn 3d orbitals40. The semiempirical DFT-D3 method was used to include the van der Waals interaction41. For MnPS3 calculations, a centered 9×9×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was used42. To eliminate periodic boundary effects, the vacuum space between adjacent slabs was set to exceed 15 Å along the z direction. Using the conjugate gradient method, the plane lattice constant and atomic coordinates were fully relaxed until the energy and force converged to 10−6 and 10−2 eV/Å, respectively. The Berry-phase method was employed to evaluate polarization magnitude43, and the ferroelectric transition switching pathway was obtained using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method44. The spin-resolved charge conductivity was calculated using Boltzmann transport theory within the constant-relaxation-time approximation as implemented in the Wannier90 package45, with the electronic temperature and relaxation time set to 300 K and 1 ps, respectively. The lattice structure was visualized using VESTA46.

“coupling” refers to the mutual influence between these properties. This distinction is now more

Altermagnetic multiferroics—materials that simultaneously host altermagnetic and
ferroelectric orders—represent a new frontier in the design of strongly coupled magnetoelectric
systems.1-4 Conventional multiferroics are often limited by the inherent separation between the
coexisting ferroelectric and magnetic orders, resulting in weak magnetoelectric coupling that
typically depends on spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as an indirect mediator.5,6 In contrast,
altermagnetic multiferroics feature opposite spin sublattices within the crystal lattice, which are
connected by rotation or mirror symmetries, while prohibiting connection through translational or
inversion symmetries.7-15 This gives rise to momentum-space spin splitting in the compensated
magnetic ordering, which is naturally compatible with the inversion symmetry breaking induced
by the ferroelectric. Central to this is the spatial symmetry, which serves as a key parameter for
geometrically coupling the spin-split electronic bands of altermagnets with the switchable
ferroelectric polarization, bypassing the reliance on SOC. This intrinsic symmetry coupling offers
a direct route to achieving robust magnetoelectric responses, fulfilling the critical requirements
for next-generation spintronic memory and logic devices.16-27
Recent theoretical studies have shown that in various low-dimensional and three-dimensional
altermagnetic multiferroic materials, ferroelectric switching can reversibly modulate the spin
texture without altering the global magnetic ordering.28-32 This offers an ideal platform for electric-
field control of spin states and highlights promising prospects for low-power, nonvolatile spintronic
applications. However, it is important to note that this coupling is subject to strict symmetry
constraints. For example, in some altermagnetic multiferroics, it has been found that the switching of
ferroelectric polarization does not affect the spin electronic bands of the altermagnetic.29,31 This
suggests that the coexistence of ferroelectric and altermagnetic does not necessarily lead to their
coupling, and the symmetry conditions that govern whether such coupling occurs remain unclear.

Sun and co-workers present a symmetry analysis enabling the prediction of couplings between
spins and ferroelectric displacements in altermagnets. They identify three different types of
coupling: a first mechanism in which spins and ferroelectric displacements are decoupled, and two
additional paths in which polarization reversal can reverse the spin texture. Using these couplings,
they further demonstrate that, in one of these mechanisms, the spin texture can generate a finite

## Paper

## Abstract

Altermagnetic multiferroics, hosting coexisting spin-splitting bands and ferroelectric polarization, offer a promising route to magnetoelectric coupling beyond conventional relativistic spin–orbit mechanism. However, the lack of a unified principle connecting ferroelectric switching symmetry to spin-band topology has impeded rational material design. Here, we establish a universal symmetry-based framework that classifies all possible spin–ferroelectric couplings in altermagnets into three fundamental types: decoupling, pseudo-time-reversal coupling, and asymmetric momentum mapping. This classification stems directly from the relation between ferroelectric switching operators and the spin Laue group, creating a decisive symmetry-to-function paradigm. First-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 confirm the framework, showing that 3 distinct ferroelectric switching paths produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions and discriminable electrical transport signatures. The universality of the framework is further validated in BiFeO3. Our work provides a predictive design principle for voltage-programmable spintronics, effectively transforming ferroelectric symmetry from a structural descriptor into a dynamic functional control knob for altermagnetic spin states.

---

## Introduction

Altermagnetic multiferroics—materials that simultaneously host altermagnetic and ferroelectric orders—represent a new frontier in the design of strongly coupled magnetoelectric systems1–4. Conventional multiferroics are often limited by the inherent separation between the coexisting ferroelectric and magnetic orders, resulting in weak magnetoelectric coupling that typically depends on spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as an indirect mediator5,6. In contrast, altermagnetic multiferroics feature opposite spin sublattices within the crystal lattice, which are connected by rotation or mirror symmetries, while prohibiting connection through translational or inversion symmetries7–15. This gives rise to momentum-space spin splitting in the compensated magnetic ordering, which is naturally compatible with the inversion symmetry breaking induced by the ferroelectric. Central to this is the spatial symmetry, which serves as a key parameter for geometrically coupling the spin-split electronic bands of altermagnets with the switchable ferroelectric polarization, bypassing the reliance on SOC. This intrinsic symmetry coupling offers a direct route to achieving robust magnetoelectric responses, fulfilling the critical requirements for next-generation spintronic memory and logic devices16–27.

Recent theoretical studies have shown that in various low-dimensional and three-dimensional altermagnetic multiferroic materials, ferroelectric switching can reversibly modulate the spin texture without altering the global magnetic ordering28–32. This offers an ideal platform for electric-field control of spin states and highlight promising prospects for low-power, nonvolatile spintronic applications. However, it is important to note that this coupling is subject to strict symmetry constraints. For example, in some altermagnetic multiferroics, it has been found that the switching of ferroelectric polarization does not affect the spin electronic bands of the altermagnetic29,31. This suggests that the coexistence of ferroelectric and altermagnetic does not necessarily lead to their coupling, and the symmetry conditions that govern whether such coupling occurs remain unclear. More fundamentally, a unified theoretical framework is still lacking to systematically describe how ferroelectric switching modulates altermagnetic spin splitting. In particular, symmetry-based classification criteria that can predict spin responses under different switching operations remain underdeveloped, hindering rational material design and functional optimization.

To address this gap, we develop a group-theoretic classification of spin–ferroelectric coupling in altermagnets. Our analysis identifies three fundamental response types—Type I: spin–ferroelectric decoupling, and Type II: pseudo-time-reversal (pseudo-spin-flip) coupling, and Type III: non-symmetric momentum mapping—each determined by the relationship between the ferroelectric switching operator and the crystal’s spin Laue group. These theoretical predictions are first confirmed through first-principles calculations on bilayer MnPS3 and subsequently validated in BiFeO3 as a prototypical 3D system, in which distinct ferroelectric switching paths are shown to produce characteristic spin-band reconstructions.

This work establishes a unified symmetry-guided framework for understanding and designing altermagnetic multiferroics with tailored magnetoelectric functionality. The distinct spin-band reconstructions further give rise to discriminable electrical transport signatures, enabling simple electrical measurements to serve as direct experimental fingerprints of the three symmetry-determined coupling types. Thus, the framework not only offers fundamental theoretical insight but also provides a practical material platform for the development of voltage-programmable, low-power spintronic devices.

In bulk BiFeO3, the R3c crystal structure arises from Pm3 m by the condensation of two primary order parameters: a polar distortion along the [111] direction and a rotation of the oxygen octahedra along the [111] direction, described by the R+ 4 irreducible representation. For polarization switching achieved by independent displacement of Bi3+ ions (referred to as path 1), the overall effect is equivalent to an inversion operation O =I, i.e., [E||I]P=P’ (Fig. 5b). However, in certain conditions, polarization switching maybe accompanied by the rotation of the oxygen octahedra (referred to as path 2)34. In this case, inversion symmetry cannot map the lattice structure while preserving the system’s magnetic ordering; instead, path 2 affects the system in an O =C 2[-110] manner, i.e., [E||C 2[-110]]P=P’ (Fig. 5b). According to Equation 9, the path 1, where O H, does not alter the spin splitting during polarization reversal, and is classified as Type I (decoupled). Path 2, where O AH, maps the opposite spin channels and is classified as Type II (pseudo-time-reversal coupling). The band structure calculations shown in Fig. 5 clearly confirm these two distinct responses.

This analysis not only emphasizes that the spin splitting control in BiFeO3 is directly related to octahedral rotation rather than polarization switching, providing an intuitive symmetry perspective for electric control of spin splitting in BiFeO3, but also clarifies the universal applicability of this symmetry mechanism in various multiferroic materials. By identifying the symmetry of the ferroelectric switching operation, one can predict and classify its magnetoelectric coupling functionality, independent of the specific system under study.

## Methods

The atomic properties and electronic structure of the materials were calculated using first-principles simulations within density functional theory (DFT)35,36. The projected augmented wave pseudopotentials method, as implemented in the Vienna Abinitio Simulation Package (VASP)37,38 was employed. The exchange-correlation energy was calculated using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form39, and the plane wave cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. A Hubbard U =4 eV with the Dudarev parametrization was applied to properly describe the localization of Mn 3d orbitals40. The semiempirical DFT-D3 method was used to include the van der Waals interaction41. For MnPS3 calculations, a centered 9×9×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was used42. To eliminate periodic boundary effects, the vacuum space between adjacent slabs was set to exceed 15 Å along the z direction. Using the conjugate gradient method, the plane lattice constant and atomic coordinates were fully relaxed until the energy and force converged to 10−6 and 10−2 eV/Å, respectively. The Berry-phase method was employed to evaluate polarization magnitude43, and the ferroelectric transition switching pathway was obtained using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method44. The spin-resolved charge conductivity was calculated using Boltzmann transport theory within the constant-relaxation-time approximation as implemented in the Wannier90 package45, with the electronic temperature and relaxation time set to 300 K and 1 ps, respectively. The lattice structure was visualized using VESTA46.
